I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
A place to wake up
There was enough morning for everyone.
CITY OF TOMO
05

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
01
The morning had room
The first thing Mira noticed was the sound of water. It passed beneath her
window with the unhurried confidence of something that would still be there
tomorrow. Beyond it, the city opened in terraces of green: beans climbing
balconies, fruit trees shading doorways, gardens where she remembered
roads ought to be.
She had arrived the night before with a small bag and an old habit of
worrying. Even now, sunlight on the quilt, she was counting the things a day
could demand of her. Rent. Breakfast. A reason to justify resting.
Somewhere a bird began an extravagant song without explaining its
usefulness.
At the garden gate, a little robot was waiting for a snail to cross the path. Its
cream shell held the morning light. Two amber eyes shone above four sturdy
wheels; a slender arm kept a watering nozzle still.
“That is TOMO,” said Leela from the neighboring balcony. “Come down
when you are ready.”
Mira looked for the urgency inside the invitation. There was none. The kettle
was warm. The garden was awake. For the first time in years, the morning
seemed to have room for her.
There was enough morning for everyone.
CITY OF TOMO
06

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
02
Breakfast belonged to the day
Under an arbor heavy with grapes, breakfast was already happening.
Someone was tearing warm bread. A humanoid with flour on its forearms
carried a tray of idlis from a kitchen fragrant with ginger. A tiny delivery
robot arrived with strawberries, taking the last corner very seriously.
Mira reached into her bag. Leela touched her wrist lightly. “You can leave
that there.”
“How does this work?”
Leela told her about an old comparison: the city as a cruise ship. People had
once paid into a common system through taxes, then paid again at the
moment they needed to eat. The first neighborhoods had begun by making
shared provision visible. You had already helped provide the kitchen;
breakfast did not need a second gate.
Here, generations later, the comparison had become an old story. No one
carried money. The gardens, kitchens, water, homes, and machines were
held in common. Resources were counted carefully, but people did not have
prices attached to them.
Mira accepted a bowl of fruit. Its sweetness was ordinary. The strange part
was the absence of a calculation afterward. Across the table, a child offered
her the larger half of a peach.
Hunger met a table, and the table had a place.
CITY OF TOMO
07

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
03
Where the streets went
The old road descended beneath an orchard. Leela led Mira to an overlook
where a glass wall revealed the city below: quiet electric vehicles moving
through ventilated tunnels, freight traveling separately, maintenance
machines inspecting the walls. Emergency routes and accessible entrances
were marked clearly. Underground life had its own patient order.
Above them, clover softened the ground once surrendered to traffic. A
narrow river curved between gardens. You could float along its gentle
current or choose a dry pod that followed the water, close a transparent
canopy, and read. Paths ran beside it for wheels and feet, with bridges,
resting places, and ways out wherever people needed them.
Mira chose a pod. On its seat lay a book someone had finished and left for
whoever came next. There was no advertisement on the canopy. The city did
not ask her to buy anything while she traveled through it.
At the next bridge, a river guardian was checking a depth sensor. A storm
upstream could change the afternoon; the pretty water was still water. The
pod slowed near a family crossing.
Under the trees, time stopped resembling a thing she was forever late to
catch.
The surface belonged to living.
CITY OF TOMO
08

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
The smallest beginning
One garden. A remembered place. A gentle action.
CITY OF TOMO

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
04
A small robot, a particular plant
TOMO stopped beside a tomato plant with a bent bamboo stake. Mira would
have called it one plant among many. TOMO knew it as the same living
neighbor it had visited yesterday.
The little robot looked at the leaves, approached the root zone, and lowered
a probe. Its arms could extend and fold, precise enough to work among
stems; its wheels carried it over the garden path. It did not rush through the
bed as though speed were kindness.
Beside a rosemary bush stood a modest green box. “That is the garden
node,” Leela said. “It keeps the history here.”
TOMO had brought the newest observation. The node remembered recent
watering and rain, the plant's location, and an earlier reading that had
seemed uncertain. Today's task allowed another measurement before any
water was given. TOMO waited, measured again, and dispensed a small
recorded amount.
Later, it would return to see what had changed. Care included the afterward.
Mira watched the nozzle lift without touching the leaves. The whole city
suddenly seemed hidden inside this exchange: a place remembered, a need
considered, an action taken gently, and someone returning to find out
whether it helped.
The smallest complete beginning was a garden.
CITY OF TOMO
10

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
05
Many shapes of kindness
There were many robots like TOMO. They were not copies arranged in
descending order of importance. Each had a body suited to somewhere and
something.
A low, broad machine carried mulch without sinking deeply into the soft
path. A tall orchard robot reached fruit that a child could only point at. Small
floating machines read the pond. A quiet crawler inspected pipes.
Humanoids worked where hands, stairs, and familiar tools made a
human-shaped body useful: kneading dough, repairing shutters, changing
the linen in a guest room.
The heavy hauling, repetitive cleaning, dangerous inspection, and tireless
tending belonged to this varied company. People still made things with their
hands. Someone spent a whole morning shaping a bowl badly and happily. A
woman weeded because she liked the smell of disturbed soil. Nobody needed
to turn pleasure into employment to defend the time it took.
At a workshop, Mira saw TOMO's arm laid open beside a larger robot's
wrist. Both could be repaired. Parts were labeled, instructions available,
tools shared.
There was affection in the machines' design, and also practicality. A city that
trusted robots with its daily care had made room for their maintenance.
Different bodies carried the same promise of care.
CITY OF TOMO

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
A question in the field
The next generation grows among living things.
CITY OF TOMO
12

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
06
The classroom without a bell
By midmorning the children were in the bean field. One was measuring
shade with a companion robot. Another had discovered a beetle and
overturned the lesson by asking where the beetle slept.
Their teacher followed the question. Soon there were sketches of shelters, a
discussion of leaves, and a small disagreement about whether shade could
be measured with a ruler. The robot brought yesterday's observations. It
could hold a magnifying lens steady; it could not decide which question a
child ought to love.
Under the pavilion were books, quiet rooms, tactile models, and tables for
anyone who preferred them. Reading, mathematics, history, and careful
experiments were woven through the day. Some children wanted a
predictable lesson. Others needed movement or a softer place to sit. The city
had many doors into learning.
Mira remembered rows of desks and the fear of giving the wrong answer too
slowly. Here a child could say, “I do not understand,” and the day widened
around the sentence.
A boy asked whether robots could grow tomatoes on the Moon. His teacher
handed him a notebook. “What would a tomato need there?”
The bean field became a doorway to space.
A question was allowed to change the afternoon.
CITY OF TOMO

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
07
The garden listened
Near the experimental beds, music drifted from a low speaker hidden
beneath a shelter. A girl called Nila had chosen the melody for the morning:
slow notes, almost transparent, threaded through the leaves.
“Is it for us?” Mira asked.
“For us too,” Nila said. The garden researchers were studying whether
particular sound treatments changed particular plants' responses. Beside
the musical bed was a quiet comparison bed, growing under otherwise
similar conditions. The notes in Nila's notebook were more cautious than her
enthusiasm.
Elsewhere, a small enclosure tested targeted acoustic signals as a way to
discourage a specific pest. If a treatment did not help, or disturbed other
creatures, they stopped it. Flowers, screens, careful observation, and
beneficial insects remained part of the garden's care. There was no promise
that one frequency could protect every crop.
Mira liked this unexpected tenderness toward uncertainty. Even in a city
built from a dream, the gardeners did not ask a tomato to prove their
favorite idea correct.
They sat awhile beneath the speakers. Beyond the trial beds, birds kept their
own arrangements. The garden was full of sound, and enough silence to hear
what answered.
Wonder could keep a notebook.
CITY OF TOMO

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
An evening beside the water
A table, a melody, a place to belong.
CITY OF TOMO

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
08
A table at the water
For the evening, Leela reserved a table beneath the pink lanterns. The
reservation held a place and told the kitchen how many people were coming.
It did not hold a payment.
“What if everyone wants the same table?” Mira asked.
“Then we take turns.” Leela smiled. “The view survives until tomorrow.”
Popular evenings used a fair rotation; unclaimed places reopened. No family
had a permanent claim on the water simply because its name was familiar.
The pond held silver fish and the wavering reflection of a moon not yet
bright enough to be certain of itself. A floating guardian checked oxygen and
temperature. A kitchen robot brought soup made with tomatoes from the
morning garden. Mira recognized their sweetness and felt, absurdly, as if
she had been introduced to an old friend.
At the far end of the terrace, musicians began tuning. People arrived without
tickets, carrying shawls and sleepy children. The music was available at the
point of showing up.
Nobody hurried them away when the bowls were empty. The table could be
used for conversation. The city had planned for that kind of occupancy too.
An evening did not need to become a transaction.
CITY OF TOMO
16

I · A PLACE TO WAKE UP
09
The rain arrived early
The first drops darkened the tablecloth before the forecast expected them. A
pond node had already noticed rising water upstream. Its message traveled
to a bridge guardian and then to the river district, carrying a time, a place,
and the uncertainty of the reading.
Pods were redirected before the lowest landing closed. A humanoid offered
an arm to an older man on the wet steps. The musicians moved under the
pavilion, laughing as they rescued a drum. Beneath the orchard, tunnel
crews checked drainage and barriers.
TOMO paused its watering task. Rain near the concert did not prove rain
had reached every tomato root; the garden node would wait for local
evidence. Until then, an old plan could remain unfinished.
Mira watched a child lean into her mother's coat. The city was beautiful in
the rain, but its beauty came partly from the things that were allowed to
interrupt it: a warning, a changed route, a machine stopping rather than
pretending to know.
By the time the music resumed, everyone had a dry place. Water gathered in
the rain gardens. The pond took the sky in widening circles.
Being cared for included being allowed to change the plan.
CITY OF TOMO

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
The intelligence of care
Memory stays close to the place it serves.
CITY OF TOMO
18

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
10
The box beside the rosemary
The next morning, Leela opened the node's weatherproof cabinet. Inside
were a computer, memory, and connections laid out with the neatness of a
well-kept kitchen drawer. Some nodes carried a GPU for heavier perception
and inference. Smaller gardens needed less.
Mira had expected a buried installation stretching beneath every plant. This
garden's node sat on a raised pad beside the path. No trench had been
opened for its data connection. Local wireless carried ordinary messages,
and the dock offered another way to exchange them.
That simplicity had made the first garden easier to begin. It had not erased
the ordinary needs of a computer outdoors. The cabinet had a tested power
supply, cooling, seals, drainage clearance, and an accessible place for
repair. Its placement respected heat, rain, and the possibility of floodwater.
Leela checked a filter while she spoke.
From outside, the box looked almost shy. It did not need to resemble a
monument to remember the garden faithfully.
TOMO approached with the latest leaf images. A long history remained in
one place while a small body moved among living things.
The brain on the ground could be an ordinary box.
CITY OF TOMO
19

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
11
What, when, and how
The morning's plan was waiting: inspect the shaded bed, revisit the
uncertain probe, water only where fresh evidence supported it, return
before the battery reserve became too small.
The node owned the what and when. It held the garden's history, estimated
its condition, and scheduled attention. TOMO owned the tactical work:
finding a traversable approach, avoiding a hose, positioning its arm,
measuring, and stopping if anything was wrong.
“The node does not steer every wheel?” Mira asked.
“No. A child might step into the path before a message could come back.”
Immediate movement and safety lived onboard. Motor and pump controls
had their own watchdogs. A mission contained limits and an expiry, not an
unlimited instruction to keep trying.
At the pond, the same relationship appeared in another body. Its node
watched trends and scheduled checks; a floating robot chose how to move
around reeds. Along the road below, a guardian tracked hazards while
inspection machines handled their own approach.
The pattern was distributed intelligence made tangible: memory rooted in
place, capable bodies carrying out bounded tasks, each with enough
independence to refuse an unsafe moment.
A goal could travel without every movement traveling with it.
CITY OF TOMO
20

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
12
The map beneath the leaves
Leela showed Mira the garden map. It held paths, slopes, bed edges, docking
places, and the space a robot needed to turn. Beside it was a world graph: a
different view of the same garden, made of things and their relationships.
This tomato belonged to that bed. That probe measured this root zone.
Yesterday's water came from this task. The graph remembered identity and
connection; the navigation map described geometry. A shared coordinate
frame let the two speak about the same place.
TOMO's destination was beside the tomato, where its arm could reach.
Driving to the plant's exact position would be a very poor interpretation of
visiting it.
Leaves grew. A chair moved. Rain made one patch slippery. TOMO reused
its map and updated what had changed, combining observations with
movement estimates while watching for wheel slip and uncertain location.
Mira began to understand spatial intelligence as a kind of practical courtesy.
It was knowing the space between a wheel and a stem, a person and a
turning arm, a destination and a possible way to arrive.
Knowing where a thing was became meaningful when you also knew how to
approach it.
A place was more than a picture of itself.
CITY OF TOMO
21

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
13
A seed receives an address
At the sowing bed, a robot made a small opening in prepared soil. The node
created a planting-site record before there was anything green to recognize.
Location, variety, date, and care instructions belonged to that beginning.
Days later, emergence would be observed and linked to the same site. A
missing seedling would remain a question in the record rather than vanish
beneath a new photograph. The plant could change its shape without losing
its story.
TOMO's observations carried their own identities too. A measurement
included units, source, quality, and the time the condition was observed. The
time the node received it was kept separately. A reading collected yesterday
and delivered today could teach the history without masquerading as the
present.
“So the garden can remember being wrong?” Mira asked.
Leela nodded. Estimates were marked as estimates; raw readings remained
distinct from interpretations. If the clock had been uncertain, that
uncertainty traveled with the event.
At the edge of the bed, Nila pressed a seed into her palm and studied its
small, improbable shape. In the city's memory it would have an address. In
her notebook it would have a drawing.
Identity let care continue through change.
CITY OF TOMO
22

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
14
The garden that could say
perhaps
A plant looked thirsty after rain. TOMO's camera showed drooping leaves; its
soil probe suggested wet ground. The node held both observations without
forcing them into one comfortable answer.
Perhaps the sensor was poorly placed. Perhaps drainage differed across the bed.
Perhaps the leaves were responding to something a photograph could not reveal.
The next visit was chosen to separate explanations: another measurement at a
checked depth, an inspection of the probe, attention to the root-zone conditions.
The node used a modest water-balance model before it used anything elaborate.
Water delivered, rain reaching the soil, estimated loss, and drainage contributed
to a prediction. Later observations could disagree. The disagreement was useful.
Similar past cases could be retrieved through vector representations, with the
search narrowed to relevant plants and conditions. The world graph linked each
case to its evidence and outcome. Resemblance alone never opened the valve.
“Does it understand why?” Mira asked.
“Sometimes it has a useful explanation. Sometimes it has a useful next
question.”
TOMO took the second reading. The garden could bear a little uncertainty more
safely than it could bear an answer invented to end it.
Knowing what to ask could be a form of intelligence.
CITY OF TOMO
23

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
15
The afternoon the radio went
quiet
One afternoon the wireless connection failed. TOMO did not become an empty
shell. Its current tasks, limits, expiry times, and completed-action records were
stored onboard, where a restart would not erase them.
It finished a permitted inspection. A watering instruction needed fresh
authorization, so that task waited. The robot kept enough energy for its return
and followed its own map toward the dock, stopping once for a fallen branch and
once because its position estimate needed checking.
At the dock, a local reference guided the final approach. Contact confirmed
arrival. Charging began, and a data-capable connector exchanged the records
that the radio had not carried. A glowing charger alone would not have done that
work.
The node and robot reconciled task identities and actual outcomes. One
interrupted action had an uncertain delivered quantity. It was marked for
assessment instead of being repeated as though nothing had happened.
Mira stood under the shed roof while rain tapped the panels. Return paths could
be blocked; connectors needed cleaning; machines could still fail. The dock was
a second path, maintained and tested.
On the screen, an unfinished task remained visibly unfinished. That honesty
protected the plant.
Memory remained when the conversation paused.
CITY OF TOMO
24

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
16
Guardians of their patches
The pond node knew the rhythm of its water: temperature across a day,
oxygen after a warm night, the level at which a landing should close. It did
not pretend to know the tomato bed better than the garden node did.
A roadside node remembered loose debris and drainage near its own bend.
An orchard node watched fruit and branch conditions. Tiny sensors
contributed observations; more capable boxes maintained local models. A
larger neighborhood machine helped with heavier computation when
invited.
Size followed local need. A node could be a small sensor, a weatherproof
computer, or a data center. Those were different responsibilities, not ranks
in a society of machines.
Nearby nodes could relay useful information. Groups could choose
temporary leaders for a shared task, then reorganize when conditions
changed. No single master had to watch every leaf on the planet.
The flood warning needed to travel. A private conversation in a home did
not. Permission, freshness, and relevance shaped each exchange. A
guardian's task was bounded care for a place, never ownership of the people
passing through it.
From the bridge, Mira saw the modest cabinets scattered among the trees.
The city was full of remembering, and still had room for privacy.
Each patch had attention close at hand.
CITY OF TOMO
25

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
17
A planetary nervous system
On the workshop wall, Nila had drawn the city as a constellation. Garden
met pond, pond met river, river met another district beyond the page. Each
mark held a local story; each line meant something worth sharing.
The builders called the wider pattern a planetary nervous system. It joined
locally grounded intelligence without requiring every reading to pass
through one distant brain. A weather change could travel toward the
gardens it affected. An observation could carry its source and uncertainty
along with its content.
The world as a graph made relationships explicit. Vector retrieval helped
find similar experiences. Spatial maps made action possible. Models
predicted change, and recorded outcomes gave those predictions something
to answer to.
Boundaries mattered. Two nodes might disagree about the rain because rain
truly differed between them. A stale message could be refused. A private
node could share a flood warning while keeping its other records local.
Mira traced a line on the drawing. It crossed a district boundary, then
stopped at a small green circle labeled only by Nila's careful picture of a
tree.
However far the network reached, somewhere it had to be right about a
particular patch of ground.
The planet could be connected without forgetting its places.
CITY OF TOMO
26

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
18
The city kept enough memory
The archive did not keep every image forever. Ordinary repeated
observations became summaries after their useful detail had been extracted.
Important changes and action records stayed long enough to investigate
trouble. Models carried versions and a record of where their evidence came
from.
The first garden had used a small database for readings, relationships, tasks,
and history. More elaborate services arrived only when a measured need
justified them. Cloud archives could help, but the root-zone decision did not
depend on a distant server remaining awake.
In the workshop, heat, power, and storage were measured as patiently as
water. A GPU was useful where its work justified its energy and cooling.
TOMO carried the computation its navigation and immediate safety
required. Sharing longer-term planning at a node could help several robots,
but the builders counted the whole arrangement before calling it a saving.
Mira liked the care given to such unromantic numbers. A city of tenderness
still needed spare parts, clean connectors, working batteries, and room to
repair things.
Outside, TOMO carried yesterday's outcome back to the garden. The archive
could become smaller without the city becoming forgetful.
Enough was a thoughtful design choice.
CITY OF TOMO
27

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
19
How the beautiful stayed
possible
The city's resource room had no price board. It showed water reserves, food
stores, energy, repair capacity, and the condition of shared equipment.
Removing money had not removed weather, materials, or the hours a machine
needed to recharge.
Orchards and fields fed the kitchens. Cooking robots planned batches around
reservations and likely arrivals, leaving room for guests who had made no plan
at all. Distribution machines brought food close to where people lived. Surpluses
were preserved; losses were recorded so the next season could be wiser.
Electricity came from a maintained mix of local generation, storage, and
connected supply. Homes, clinics, gardens, and workshops shared priorities
agreed in public. Water moved through treatment and reuse systems suited to
its next purpose. The river's beauty belonged to that accounting too: flow,
cleanliness, access, flood protection, energy.
During a poor harvest, kitchens changed menus. Scarce experiences used fair
turns. Basic provision did not disappear because someone had less influence or
had contributed less visibly.
Mira watched a cook taste a different soup from the one planned. It was good.
The city had learned that abundance needed stewardship, and stewardship could
arrive without a bill.
The dream still knew where its water came from.
CITY OF TOMO
28

II · HOW THE PLACE REMEMBERS
20
The first garden was smaller
In the oldest workshop was a photograph of the first trial bed. No river city
stood behind it. There were a few tomato plants, a marked path, a node, a
dock, and a robot being watched by a person with a notebook.
The first proof was a complete loop: find the same plant again, gather a
trustworthy observation, deliver a controlled amount of water, record the
result, and return. Sowing and skilled harvesting belonged to later work,
after movement and watering could be trusted.
The builders tested sensors and delivered volume at the bench. They
measured navigation, docking, and unwanted contacts. In shadow mode,
proposed care decisions were compared with a simple baseline before the
robot controlled watering. They deliberately disconnected the radio and
tested the return, the pause, the physical synchronization, and the handling
of uncertain actions.
Two nodes exchanged one useful update before anyone spoke confidently
about a planetary network. Acceptance criteria came before the trial; results
included conditions, failures, and human interventions.
Mira leaned closer to the photograph. The imagined city had begun with a
task small enough to finish and a record honest enough to improve.
TOMO was the smallest complete instance. The city grew from learning what
that instance needed.
One tended tomato could contain a direction.
CITY OF TOMO
29

III · BEYOND THE HORIZON
Toward the stars
The generation that builds for the spacefaring generation.
CITY OF TOMO
30

III · BEYOND THE HORIZON
21
The generation that planted
departure
The observatory was built above a greenhouse. To reach the stars in the evening,
the children first walked past tomatoes in warm rows.
Their models of distant habitats were full of familiar questions. Where would
water return? What happened when a sensor failed? Could a robot find its dock
without a message from Earth? How would a small community keep a shared
memory through a long interruption?
The generation building the city understood itself as preparing for a spacefaring
generation. Some would never leave Earth. They still worked on reliable care,
closed material cycles, repairable machines, and intelligence that could live
close to what it served.
In Nila's model, an orbital node remembered the greenhouse while a small
TOMO tended its plants. Other nodes marked stations and service points. A
traveling craft could carry its own world model and exchange useful local
information when it reached another place.
Mira looked from the model to the real vines below the glass. The scale had
changed, but care remained particular: this reservoir, this valve, this leaf
turning toward a lamp.
The children were building a route outward with skills first learned while
keeping something alive nearby.
A garden could be an apprenticeship to the stars.
CITY OF TOMO
31

III · BEYOND THE HORIZON
22
Stations in the dark
In the dream Nila described, a spacecraft approached a small service station
with the unhurried precision of TOMO returning to its shed. It had traveled
on stored plans, watched its reserves, and carried a record of the journey.
A satellite node held local traffic information, docking references, and the
condition of available equipment. The craft checked the message and its age
before trusting it. Another station, farther on, had its own memory and its
own limits.
At a compatible dock, energy could pass from a station's power system into
the craft's storage. Some journeys required propellant or other supplies
instead; a node could coordinate a service only where the actual hardware
and resources existed. Nothing in the dark was fed by intelligence alone.
Inside the little greenhouse, a robot inspected a tomato plant. Earth was a
blue curve beyond the window. Mira imagined a person tasting that first ripe
fruit far from rain.
The chain of places would never abolish distance. It could make distance
more habitable: a reliable arrival, an honest record, a repair, a supply
waiting where a previous generation had placed it.
Even among the stars, someone would need to check the seal.
The future could leave a light on for the next arrival.
CITY OF TOMO
32

III · BEYOND THE HORIZON
23
The things we chose to carry
At the departure exhibition, the children were asked what a city should send
into space. Their first answers were practical: water systems, seeds, tools,
spare parts, medical supplies, power, maps.
Then a girl added music. Someone else wanted a library in many languages.
Nila drew a long table. A boy wrote that every habitat should have a window
where a person could sit without needing to do anything useful.
Mira thought of the generations who might build such places and never see
them. They would leave diagrams, tested joints, repaired assumptions, and
ways to share a small world without making every shortage an excuse for
power.
The city's machines could do its necessary labor. They could not decide on
humanity's behalf what deserved its freed hours. Those hours belonged to
friendship, discovery, grief, play, art, contemplation, and forms of care no
sensor could fully describe.
Under the greenhouse glass, a teacher tied a child’s loose shoelace while a
companion robot held the notebook dry. The gesture was too small for the
exhibition wall. Mira thought it might be the most valuable thing there.
A spacefaring generation would inherit whatever its elders practiced close to
home.
Kindness was something to learn before departure.
CITY OF TOMO
33

IV · WHAT REMAINS BETWEEN US
24
The old habit at the table
It happened during a small gathering after the concert. Someone asked who
had contributed most to the river restoration. The question was warm,
almost casual. Soon names began collecting around it.
Mira felt the familiar movement inside herself: the wish to be mentioned, the
fear of having done too little, the tiny calculation of where she stood among
the others. Money had vanished from the table. Comparison had found an
empty chair and sat down.
One of the river builders paused. “There were people who did things nobody
saw,” she said. “And people who could not join us this season.”
They spoke of the work: which planting held the bank, which approach
failed, what should be repaired next. They thanked people by name where
thanks belonged. They did not turn the gratitude into a list of better and
lesser lives.
The moment passed, but Mira kept it. A beautiful city could not depend on
everyone becoming perfectly generous. It would need ways to notice when
admiration hardened into rank, and ways to loosen it again.
Across the water, a robot was clearing the last chairs. The difficult part of
the evening had required no machine.
The old hunger for a higher place could still visit.

IV · WHAT REMAINS BETWEEN US

Glory with nowhere to buy a gate
Leela had helped design the earliest kitchens. People loved her for it. She
could tell a story and gather a crowd without raising her voice. Mira
wondered whether influence might become the city's next currency.
“It can,” Leela said. “We have to pay attention.”
The people who changed a food schedule did not gain the right to decide
who deserved dinner. A celebrated builder could not reserve the waterfront
forever. Technical authority was limited to a task, recorded, reviewed, and
passed on. Decisions that affected common life had routes for challenge.
There were no contribution scores following people from place to place. The
city's records could measure a pump's reliability without measuring a
person's worth. Invitations, affection, and disagreement still existed; none
became a condition for a home or a meal.
Mira thought of how easily gratitude could become obedience when one
person controlled what another needed. Here the work was to keep thanks
free of that hidden debt.
Leela took a bowl from the kitchen shelf and washed it herself because she
was standing there. A humanoid beside her continued stacking the others.
For a moment, her much-loved name was simply the name of someone next
to a sink.
Admiration did not come with a key to anyone’s necessities.

IV · WHAT REMAINS BETWEEN US
26
The person on the bench
For several days, Mira saw the same man sitting beneath the fig tree.
Sometimes he watched the river. Sometimes he slept. She had seen no sign
of what he contributed.
The thought embarrassed her as soon as she recognized it. She had been
learning the city and had brought an old measuring instrument in her
pocket.
One afternoon she sat at the other end of the bench. The man offered a quiet
greeting. They watched a floating robot pass beneath a bridge. After a long
while he told her that his sister had died in the winter.
There was no lesson attached to the telling. He did not need grief to make
him acceptable, and she did not need to uncover a hidden achievement to
defend his place there. The bench, the fig shade, dinner later: none had been
waiting for his explanation.
When Mira left, she brought him a glass of water. She did not enter it
anywhere.
The city made contribution possible without making survival its reward. A
person could be useful, recovering, uncertain, old, young, or simply tired.
Belonging remained beneath those changing seasons.
Some days, being held was enough.

IV · WHAT REMAINS BETWEEN US

From comparing to contributing
Nila came home unhappy because another child's model bridge had worked
better than hers. She knew the city had no prizes for the best child. Her
disappointment had not received that information.
Leela sat beside her and studied the broken span. “What did you want it to
carry?”
“The little delivery robot.”
They measured its wheels. Nila asked the other child how the stronger joint had
been made. By evening the two models had become one bridge, broad enough
for the robot and beautiful enough for Nila's improbable painted flowers.
No announcement followed. Nobody declared them the city's most collaborative
children. They rolled a basket of tomatoes across and ate some of the tomatoes
afterward.
Mira watched the pleasure return to Nila's face. It had found an object in the
world: a crossing that worked, a friend beside it, something useful now
possible. That pleasure did not need someone else's failure to stay alive.
Competition had not been defeated in a grand argument. On this particular
afternoon, comparison had loosened its grip when attention moved toward what
the bridge could give.
There would be other afternoons. The city had made room to practice.
The question became: what can we make possible together?

IV · WHAT REMAINS BETWEEN US

The gate that was gone
On her last morning, Mira woke with the old fear again. It arrived before
thought: What if I am no longer wanted? What if I cannot keep up? What if
someone who dislikes me can take away the life I need?
Then she heard water beneath the window. Breakfast would be there. Her
room was hers to rest in. A disagreement yesterday had not changed her
right to care today.
She understood why the robots had never been the whole story. Their work
mattered because it helped loosen the dependence through which people
could govern one another's survival. Food, shelter, essential energy, and
access to ordinary life were shared foundations. Nobody's approval was the
private tap from which they flowed.
There were still decisions, limits, repairs, and difficult people. There were
processes to question and relationships to mend. The city had not finished
being human.
But a lever had moved. Mira could leave an unkind room without leaving the
possibility of dinner behind. She could say no. She could offer kindness
without secretly purchasing security.
At the garden gate, TOMO was waiting for the snail again. Mira sat on the
low wall and waited too.
Love had more room where fear held fewer necessities.

Make life beautiful
That evening Mira stayed. She had stopped calling the room a guest room and
placed her own small plant on the windowsill.
Below, the river carried lantern light through the gardens. A kitchen humanoid
closed a cupboard. An orchard robot came home with its empty baskets. The
pond guardian recorded a quiet reading. Somewhere beneath the trees, a node
kept the history of a day that no single machine had needed to hold entire.
TOMO returned to the tomato bed. There would be another observation
tomorrow, another changed leaf, another reason to revise a plan. There were
many robots like TOMO across the city, each bringing capable hands, wheels,
or patient movement to the care of a particular place.
At the observatory, children were looking outward. The generation building
their departure had left the greenhouse lights on. At the fig tree, someone had
set down two cups.
Mira opened her window. The city smelled of wet earth and dinner and
jasmine. She could not name a single measure that contained the value of this
evening. She did not try.
On the workshop door, almost hidden by a climbing rose, were four simple
words.
Make life beautiful.
And tomorrow, begin again with care.

About this imagined city
City of Tomo is an imagined future, written from Ilak's TOMO concepts. Its river city, shared
provision, robot capabilities, and orbital habitats are fictional scenes, not descriptions of a
completed product or a demonstrated economic system.
The engineering passages adapt TOMO: The Planetary Nervous System; its seven-slide
talking points and narrated-presentation script; and TOMO: Technical Architecture with its
seventeen-section technical talking points. These materials describe proposed architecture
and validation work. TOMO begins with supervised mapping, inspection, and controlled
watering; advanced manipulation, city-scale coordination, and space applications remain
future possibilities.
The sound-garden scenes imagine bounded experiments. They do not establish that music
improves crops or that acoustic treatments can replace chemical pest management. No
universal plant frequency or pest-control performance is claimed. The no-trench node scene
describes an installation option requiring suitable power, communications, thermal
management, protection, and maintenance. Space servicing requires physical energy and
supply infrastructure.
The book also develops the ten ideas supplied for this commission and previously shared
concepts about contribution, distributed nodes, and a spacefaring generation. Original X
posts could not be independently retrieved, so no invented post quotations or claim of a
